question.:question/problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=\operatorname{sin}⁡2t,\,y={sin}^{2}⁡t,\,0\le t<2\pi ,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{12}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t=\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡2t}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=\frac{\pi }{12},$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{12}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tan}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{6}\right) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=2{t}^{2}+3,\,y=3{t}^{5}+{t}^{3},\,0\le t<\infty ,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=1.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2}(5{t}^{2}+1).
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{3{t}^{2}(5{t}^{2}+1)}{4t}=\frac{3t(5{t}^{2}+1)}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=1,$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{3(1)(5(1)^{2}+1)}{4} \\  & =\frac{18}{4} \\  & =\frac{9}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
For the parametric curve 

$$
x=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=\frac{4}{\pi }{t}^{2},\,0\le t<2\pi ,
$$

calculate the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point where $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,{y}^{′}(t)=\frac{8}{\pi }t.
$$

 

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{(\frac{8}{\pi }t)}{4\operatorname{cos}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{2t\operatorname{sec}⁡t}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, when $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ the slope of the tangent to the curve is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dy}{dx} & =\frac{2\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)\operatorname{sec}⁡\left(\frac{\pi }{4}\right)}{\pi } \\  & =\frac{(\frac{\pi }{2}\cdot \sqrt{2})}{\pi } \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\times b & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 2x & 3 & 2 \\ x & 1 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix}i-\begin{vmatrix}2x & 2 \\ x & -1\end{vmatrix}j+\begin{vmatrix}2x & 3 \\ x & 1\end{vmatrix}k \\  & =(-3-2)i-(-2x-2x)j+(2x-3x)k \\  & =⟨-5,-4x,x⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the magnitude, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\,a\times b\,| & =\sqrt{(-5)^{2}+(-4x)^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25+16{x}^{2}+{x}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{17{x}^{2}+25}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we solve for $x$ the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\,a\times b\,| & =\sqrt{93} \\ \sqrt{17{x}^{2}+25} & =\sqrt{93} \\ 17{x}^{2}+25 & =93 \\ 17{x}^{2} & =68 \\ {x}^{2} & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=\pm 2.$

Using the determinant formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a\times b & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 2x\end{vmatrix} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 0 \\ -4 & 2x\end{vmatrix}i-\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 0 \\ 2 & 2x\end{vmatrix}j+\begin{vmatrix}-3 & 2 \\ 2 & -4\end{vmatrix}k \\  & =(4x-0)i-(-6x-0)j+(12-4)k \\  & =⟨4x,6x,8⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the magnitude, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\,a\times b\,| & =\sqrt{(4x)^{2}+(6x)^{2}+(8)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{x}^{2}+36{x}^{2}+64} \\  & =\sqrt{52{x}^{2}+64}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\,a\times b\,| & =\sqrt{77} \\ \sqrt{52{x}^{2}+64} & =\sqrt{77} \\ 52{x}^{2}+64 & =77 \\ 52{x}^{2} & =13 \\ {x}^{2} & =\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}

question.:question/problem: For which of the following vector fields is $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-y$ a potential function?
question.:question/worked-solution:
A vector field $F$ is conservative if it is the gradient of a scalar function $f.$ That is, there exists a function $f$ such that $F=∇f.$ The function $f$ is called a potential function for $F.$

To compute the vector field associated with a potential function $f,$ we compute its gradient.

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-y)\,j \\  & =2x\,i-j \\  & =F\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector field that has $f$ as a potential function is

$$
F=2x\,i-j.
$$

question.:question/problem: Consider the vector field $F=(ay-2x{y}^{3})\,i+(x-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\,j$ on ${R}^{2},$ where $a$ is a constant. Given that $F$ is conservative, find the value of $a.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j$ be a vector field with domain $D={R}^{2},$ where $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first-order partial derivatives everywhere on $D.$ Then, we have the following theorem:

$F$ *is conservative if and only if $\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}$ everywhere on $D.$*

For the vector field $F,$ we have $P=ay-2x{y}^{3}$ and $Q=x-3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=a-6x{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1-6x{y}^{2}.
$$

It's clear that the partial derivatives exist and are continuous on ${R}^{2}.$ Equating the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}a-6x{y}^{2} & =1-6x{y}^{2} \\ a & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $a=1.$

question.:question/problem: Consider the vector field $F=\frac{axy}{{x}^{2}+1}\,i+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\,j$ on ${R}^{2},$ where $a$ is a constant. Given that $F$ is conservative, find the value of $a.$

For the vector field $F,$ we have $P=\frac{axy}{{x}^{2}+1}$ and $Q=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1).$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$

It's clear that the partial derivatives exist and are continuous on ${R}^{2}.$ Equating the partial derivatives, we get

$$

$$

Therefore, we conclude that $a=2.$

$$

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F$ denotes the divergence of the vector field $F.$

Intuitively, the divergence of $F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P:$

- If $F$ acts like a source at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F>0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F<0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F=0$ at $P.$

![](images/6c/6c747149618d4c5ef35e727af15cd001365bd9c2d5e064689baf24c6ee23cff9.png)

If $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere in the domain of $F,$ we say that $F$ is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement $∇\cdot F=0$ is true, whereas statements $∇\cdot F>0$ and $∇\cdot F<0$ are false. For any point $P,$ the sum of the inward-pointing vectors equals the sum of the outward-pointing vectors. Therefore, $F$ acts neither like a source nor a sink.

- Statement “$F$ is solenoidal” is true. Since $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere, the vector field $F$ is solenoidal.

Therefore, the correct answer is $∇\cdot F=0$; “$F$ is solenoidal” only.

question.:question/problem: Given that $F=y\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,i+{x}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡y\,j,$ what is $\text{div}\,F?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j$ is a vector field on ${R}^{2}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡y) \\  & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡x-2{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
To find the Cartesian equation of the circle, we need to eliminate the parameter $\theta .$ We can do this using the Pythagorean theorem.

By isolating the $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ term in the $x$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+1 & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{2}{3}(x+1) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{4}{9}{(x+1)}^{2} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

By isolating the $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ term in the $y$-equation and squaring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+2 & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{2}{3}(y+2) & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \frac{4}{9}{(y+2)}^{2} & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding the two equations and using ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{9}{(x+1)}^{2}+\frac{4}{9}{(y+2)}^{2} & ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ 4{(x+1)}^{2}+4{(y+2)}^{2} & =9 \\ {(x+1)}^{2}+{(y+2)}^{2} & =\frac{9}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore the Cartesian equation of the circle is ${(x+1)}^{2}+{(y+2)}^{2}=\frac{9}{4}.$

$$

$$

$$
